title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: LLM review of the romanization, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The first case ending you write yourself: a feminine noun ending in -a or -ya swaps that ending for -u or -yu when it is the thing being wanted, liked or taken. vodá → vódu, kníga → knígu, múzyka → múzyku. Nothing else in the sentence moves — but watch the acute as well as the ending: vodá → vódu takes the stress with it, kníga → knígu leaves it alone, and which of the two a word does is a fact about that word.

The object does NOT always change, and M1 showed you why before this rule existed: a masculine noun naming a thing rather than a living creature (chay, khleb, sok) looks identical whether it is the subject or the object, a neuter noun (molokó) likewise, and kófe never changes at all. So "the object case changes the ending" is only true of the feminine -a/-ya nouns at this level. Learn which nouns move rather than expecting all of them to.

Negation is one word in one place: ne goes immediately in front of the verb and nothing else happens. Ya ne khochú kófe. English has to fetch an auxiliary — do not, does not, did not — and Russian has nothing of the kind, in any tense. This one word will still be doing the whole job in M5's past and M6's future.

Wanting to DO something is khochú plus the plain dictionary form of the verb, with no word for "to": Ya khochú rabótat'. English's "to" tempts a chto or a chtóby into the gap, and neither belongs there.

khotét' does not follow either of the ordinary ending patterns — it is one of a handful of Russian verbs that mix them: khochú (I), khóchet (he, she), khotíte (you, polite). Learn these three shapes as they come; M4 sorts out the verbs that DO behave.

A word borrowed whole from another language often refuses to change at all: kófe is the same in every position in every sentence. There are only a few such nouns, and they are a gift — nothing to learn.

words.note: "I want", from khotét' — a verb that mixes the two ending patterns, learned shape by shape: khochú (I), khóchet (he or she), khotíte (you). Bare it is blunt; pozháluysta makes it a request.

sentences.trap: Nothing happened to chay. After a whole module about endings it is easy to expect one here — but a masculine thing keeps its dictionary shape as the object, and that is the point of starting with this sentence.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO chai. The kh is the raspy h from khoroshó, and the o in front of the stress flattens to "a".

variations.changed: swap the drink — another masculine thing, so still nothing moves
khochú → khotíte for the polite you, and the sentence becomes a question with nothing added
pozháluysta turns the bare want into a request — the ordinary way to order something

mistake.why: cháyu is a real shape of chay, but it belongs to a different job (a partial amount — "some tea"), and this level does not teach it. Ya khochú chay.

sentences.usage: Ordering, asking, saying what you would like — add pozháluysta and it is polite anywhere.
sentences.mnemonic: Masculine things that are not alive travel light: subject or object, same shape.

words.note: Water. vodá is the dictionary and subject shape; vódu is the object shape — the first ending here you write on purpose. The stress jumps with the ending: va-DA, but VO-doo.

sentences.trap: Ya khochú vodá is the sentence an English speaker writes, because English objects never change. It is the module's whole lesson in one error: a feminine -a noun becomes -u when it is what you want.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO VO-doo. The stress moves from the ending to the front when vodá becomes vódu, which is why the two shapes barely sound alike.

variations.changed: ne in front of the verb — and the object keeps the ending it already had
the polite you-form as a question, with the object still bent
the verb dropped entirely — and the object keeps its ending, because the verb is still understood

mistake.why: vodá is the shape for the subject of a sentence. As the thing wanted it becomes vódu.

sentences.usage: Anywhere you would ask for water — a café, a shop, somebody's kitchen.
sentences.mnemonic: -a is the shape that sits still; -u is the shape something is being done to.

words.note: Book. The same swap as vodá — -a becomes -u as the object — but the stress sits still: kníga, knígu. Whether stress jumps is a fact about each word. knígi is the plural (M8).

sentences.trap: Still no word for "a". Ya khochú knígu covers "I want a book" and "I want the book" alike, and which one is meant comes from the conversation.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO KNEE-goo. Both k and n are said at the start — Russian is comfortable with the cluster English lost centuries ago.

variations.cue: I would like a book, please
variations.changed: pozháluysta makes it a request rather than a demand
khochú → khóchet: the person changes and the object keeps its ending
ne in front of the verb, and nothing else moves

mistake.why: The dictionary shape kníga is for the subject. As the thing wanted it is knígu.

sentences.usage: In a shop or a library — and the same frame does duty for anything you are asking for.
sentences.mnemonic: Every -a that gets wanted turns into -u.

words.note: "Not", immediately in front of the word it denies — almost always the verb. Nothing else changes: Russian has no do not / did not in any tense. Ne does the whole job in M5 and M6 too.
Coffee — borrowed whole, and it never changes shape in any position. It counts as masculine despite the -e that usually means neuter; you will hear the neuter too.

sentences.trap: English needs "do" to say no to something — I don't want — and hunting for its Russian equivalent is wasted effort. There is none. ne does the whole job on its own.
sentences.sound: ya nye kha-CHOO KO-fye. ne leans onto the verb and is barely a syllable of its own.

variations.changed: swap the drink — ne stays exactly where it was
drop ne and the sentence flips: nothing else has to move back
the person changes; ne still sits in front of the verb

mistake.why: That says "it is not coffee that I want" — ne denies whatever follows it, so putting it before the noun changes the meaning. To refuse, it goes in front of the verb: Ya ne khochú kófe.

sentences.usage: Turning something down — and adding spasíbo makes it polite rather than blunt.
sentences.mnemonic: ne sticks to the front of the verb like a burr; move it and you have said something else.

words.note: Bread. Masculine — it ends in a consonant — and a thing rather than a creature, so it never changes as the object. There is no word for "some" in front of it either.

words.cue: please · you're welcome · here you are
words.note: One word, three English jobs: "please" when you ask, "you're welcome" when thanked, "here you are" when handing over. It turns a bare Ya khochú … into a polite request; set off by a comma.

sentences.trap: Ya khochú on its own is blunt — closer to "I want" than to "I'd like". pozháluysta is what carries the politeness, so a request that leaves it out is a request that sounds abrupt.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO khlyep pa-ZHA-loo-sta. The final b of khleb is said as a p — Russian hardens the last consonant of a word — and the y inside pozháluysta disappears in ordinary speech.

variations.changed: drop pozháluysta and the request becomes a bare statement of what you want
the verb dropped entirely — and the object keeps its ending, because the verb is still understood
the polite you-form, asked instead of told

mistake.why: khléba is a real shape and it belongs to the "some of it" job this level does not teach. The plain object is khleb.

sentences.usage: The shop, the bakery, the table — the most ordinary request in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: pozháluysta is the whole of Russian politeness in one word — and it goes at the end.

words.note: Music. Feminine, so it takes the -u ending as the object, exactly like vodá and kníga. The stress stays on the first syllable throughout: MOO-zy-ka, MOO-zy-koo.

sentences.trap: M1 taught lyublyú with objects that never moved — chay, molokó, rússkiy yazýk. This is the same verb with a feminine object, and now the ending appears. The verb was never what decided it; the noun always was.
sentences.sound: ya lyoo-BLYOO MOO-zy-koo. Two of Russian's harder sounds in one short sentence: the soft l of lyublyú and the back y of múzyku.

variations.changed: ne in front of the verb — the M3 lesson applied to an M1 verb
lyublyú → lyúbit: the person changes and múzyku keeps its ending
the describing word bends with the noun it describes — rússkiy → rússkuyu

mistake.why: The ending belongs to the noun, not to the verb: any feminine -a noun in the object slot becomes -u, whichever verb put it there.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are fond of — the M1 frame, now with the endings it always needed.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb never decides the ending. The noun does.

words.note: The dictionary shape of "work" — the one that goes straight after khochú. Everyday shapes: rabótayu (I), rabótayete (you), rabótayet (he or she) — M4. Almost every dictionary shape ends in -t'.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "to". English "want to work" has three words and Russian has two, and the missing one has no Russian stand-in — not chto, not chtóby, nothing at all.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO ra-BO-tat'. The ' on the end of rabótat' is not a sound: it softens the t, so the word ends in a light "t" rather than a hard one.

variations.changed: swap the activity — any dictionary shape drops straight into the slot
khochú → khóchet, and rabótat' does not move: only the first verb ever changes
the polite you-form, as a question

mistake.why: The chto is English's "to", smuggled in. Nothing goes between khochú and the dictionary shape: Ya khochú rabótat'.

sentences.usage: Plans, wishes and job conversations — the most productive frame on this rung.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, no glue. The second one just stands there in its dictionary clothes.

words.note: To sleep. Its everyday shapes grow an l in the I-form only — splyu (I), spíte (you), spit (he or she) — M1's lyublyú quirk. Ya khochú spat' is how Russian says "I'm sleepy".

sentences.trap: ne lands in front of khochú, not in front of spat'. It denies the wanting, and moving it would deny the sleeping instead.
sentences.sound: ya nye kha-CHOO spat'. Three words lean together into what sounds like two; only khochú carries a real stress.

variations.changed: drop ne — and note that this positive version is how Russian says "I'm sleepy"
the person changes and ne stays in front of the first verb
swap the second verb — the negation frame takes any of them

mistake.why: That says you want to stay awake. ne denies what comes next, so it belongs in front of khochú.

sentences.usage: Turning down a nap, or saying you are not tired — and the positive Ya khochú spat' is the everyday "I'm sleepy".
sentences.mnemonic: Whatever ne touches is what gets denied. Put it where you mean it.

sentences.cue: I want to read a book

words.note: To read, a very regular verb: chitáyu (I), chitáyete (you), chitáyet (he or she) — endings hang off the -a of the stem. M4 uses it as the pattern well-behaved verbs follow.

sentences.trap: Both lessons of the module are in this one sentence and they do not interfere: chitát' stands bare after khochú, and knígu still bends because it is the thing being read. The infinitive does not protect the noun behind it.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO chee-TAT' KNEE-goo. Four unstressed syllables and two stressed ones — Russian rhythm is a series of quick steps and heavy landings.

variations.cue: I want to read a newspaper
variations.changed: swap the thing read — and the new noun bends the same way, because it is feminine too

variations.cue: I don't want to read the book
variations.changed: ne in front of the first verb; the other two words do not move

variations.cue: Anna wants to read a book
variations.changed: only khochú changes for the person — the other two words are fixed

mistake.why: kníga is still the thing being read, so it still bends: knígu. Standing behind an infinitive changes nothing.

sentences.usage: Saying what you want to do, with what — the fullest sentence this rung can build.
sentences.mnemonic: The infinitive is bare and the noun is bent. Both at once, every time.

words.note: Juice. Masculine, a thing rather than a creature, so it is the same shape everywhere — and short enough to be the easiest word on the rung.

sentences.trap: khotíte is the you-form because this course speaks vy — and vy takes the plural ending whether it means one person or a room full of them.
sentences.sound: vy kha-TEE-tye sok. The pitch rises on sok, which is the whole question: nothing was added to make it one.

variations.changed: swap the drink for a feminine one, and the ending appears: vódu
khotíte → khochú: the answer, with the same unchanged noun
ne in front of the verb — in Russian this is an ordinary offer, not a reproach

mistake.why: khóchesh' is the ty-form, and this course speaks vy. With vy the verb is khotíte, however few people you mean.

sentences.usage: Offering something — at a table, in a shop, in somebody's home.
sentences.mnemonic: vy always takes the plural ending. One person, plural verb, every time.

comprehensionPool.cue: I don't want to work, thank you
